style_prompt:
Style: warm, curious and even-handed, like a sharp documentary storyteller walking a friend through a new projection and reading it honestly as a range. Bright and forward-leaning on the opening and on the twist about the simpler average, grounded and a little firmer on the wildfire acres, generous and fair on the line that credits the paper, a dry half-smile on mostly in math, and the final question asked directly and warmly, as a real question, not a verdict. Never doom, never hype. Keep every routine pause short. Two passages are the scientist's own words, the sentence after the lead author said, and the phrase quite a large uncertainty. Read each as a quotation, a slight candid shift of voice, then straight back to the narrator.
Pace: MEASURED and unhurried, never padded. THIS IS A TWO MINUTE PIECE, about one hundred and fifteen seconds, and the read must fill it, so let every sentence land and take an easy breath at each period, a natural beat rather than a long pause. Save real rests for the marked short pauses. Do not rush the numbers. Vary the tone line to line so no two sentences sound the same.
Emphasis: lean on one key word in each line and let every number land whole, both ends of every range, never swallowed.

lines.text: By twenty-one hundred, under high emissions, Alaska could get more than double, up to nearly seven times, today's ground strikes.
lines.why: Open bright and forward-leaning, keep 'could' and 'high emissions' audible so the hook is a projection, and let 'nearly seven times' be the lift.

lines.text: That's from a new study in Earth's Future.
lines.why: Drop to an easy, informative register right after the hook so the source sounds like a fact, not a second headline.

lines.text: Andreas Krause's team built it with a machine learning model.
lines.why: A small lift on the method, the AI is the story's engine and should sound interesting, not ominous.

lines.text: It learned from six everyday weather readings, and where ground strikes landed.
lines.why: Plain and unhurried, a half-smile of wonder at how ordinary the inputs are.

lines.text: Remember this. [short pause] It trained on one year of data, twenty nineteen.
lines.why: The plant the second half pays off, so lean in to the listener, a beat after 'Remember this', and press 'one year'.

lines.text: On today's climate, most of Alaska got under one strike per square kilometer a year.
lines.why: Settle into the baseline number, calm and clear, so the jump in the next line has somewhere to rise from.

lines.text: That future could bring a hundred sixteen to five hundred ninety-four percent more.
lines.why: The range is the finding, so give both ends equal weight with a lift on the top end, slightly slower on the numbers.

lines.text: For the world's land, seventy-six to a hundred forty percent more.
lines.why: A comparison, lighter and quicker than Alaska's range, so the ear hears Alaska's as the wider one without being told.

lines.text: Lightning fires burned at least ninety-three percent of Alaska's wildfire acres every year for a decade.
lines.why: Why it reaches Alaskans, grounded, warmer and a touch slower, firm on 'at least ninety-three percent'.

lines.text: The study didn't model fire, only lightning, the spark behind those acres.
lines.why: A crisp, honest boundary line, brisk and clear so the fire context is never heard as the study's claim.

lines.text: Krause, the lead author, said, [short pause] I was quite surprised that the projections were so high.
lines.why: The turn of the film, a beat after 'said' then the scientist's own sentence read as a quote, candid and a little amused, not alarmed.

lines.text: Run backward on the nineteen hundreds, the model estimated about twelve percent more lightning per degree.
lines.why: Explainer mode, even and patient, set up 'backward' so 'forward' can answer it two sentences later.

lines.text: Earlier studies projected eight to seventeen percent per degree. Run forward, its own twelve could nearly triple, to thirty percent.
lines.why: First sentence even, then a clear shift up on 'Run forward', curious rather than accusing, with 'nearly triple' the lift.

lines.text: Per the press release, earlier studies differ from this one mostly in math. Krause calls lightning's response quite a large uncertainty.
lines.why: A dry half-smile on 'mostly in math', then quieter, setting 'quite a large uncertainty' off as the scientist's own phrase.

lines.text: A month earlier, Krause and Anja Rammig posted a preprint testing lightning models. [short pause] A simple average beat the machine learning ones.
lines.why: The second movement and the energy peak, bright genuine surprise after the beat, played as fascinating, never as a gotcha.

lines.text: Their advice, test models outside their training conditions.
lines.why: Settle from the peak into plain, useful advice, clear and unhurried, 'outside' carrying the meaning.

lines.text: In fairness, this paper says its model beat a regression and three existing formulas.
lines.why: Credit what works with real warmth and a brighter lift, so the fairness line sounds meant, not tacked on.

lines.text: Read it as a range. [short pause] Even the low end would more than double lightning in fire country.
lines.why: The line to land, grounded and slower, a beat after the instruction, a light touch on 'low end' and the weight on 'double'.

lines.text: The whole range waits on a test in weather it never saw.
lines.why: Lift slightly into curiosity, an open door rather than a warning, leading into the close.

lines.text: One June Sunday in twenty twenty-four put nearly seven thousand strikes on Alaska. [short pause] Who should run that test?
lines.why: A vivid image with 'nearly seven thousand' landing whole, a beat, then the question straight to the listener, warm and genuinely asked.
